stops.name: Tolbiac (Zülpich), the vow on the battlefield
stops.campa: In the fifteenth year of his reign war comes with the Alamanni, and in the fierce slaughter the Frankish line begins to break. Clovis sees his army in danger of destruction, raises his eyes to heaven, and with remorse in his heart bursts into tears and cries his vow to the God of Clotilde. As the words leave him, the Alamanni turn their backs and scatter; their king is killed, and the people submit, praying that no more perish: we are yours now. He stops the killing and rides home to tell the queen how Christ gave the victory. His Constantine moment; the bridge is Tolbiac.
stops.quote: Jesus Christ, whom Clotilda asserts to be the son of the living God, who art said to give aid to those in distress, and to bestow victory on those who hope in thee, I beseech the glory of thy aid, with the vow that if thou wilt grant me victory over these enemies, and I shall know that power which she says that people dedicated in thy name have had from thee, I will believe in thee and be baptized in thy name. For I have invoked my own gods but, as I find, they have withdrawn from aiding me; and therefore I believe that they possess no power, since they do not help those who obey them. I now call upon thee, I desire to believe thee, only let me be rescued from my adversaries.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.30 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Reims, the secret instruction by Saint Remigius
stops.campa: The queen asks Saint Remi, bishop of Reims, to summon the king secretly and open to him the word of salvation. The bishop urges him to believe in the true God, maker of heaven and earth, and to cease worshipping idols that help no one. The king hears gladly but fears his people will not abandon their gods; he will go and speak to them. He meets his followers, and before he can open his mouth the power of God anticipates him: all the people cry out together, O pious king, we reject our mortal gods, and we are ready to follow the immortal God whom Remi preaches.
stops.quote: I gladly hear you, most holy father; but there remains one thing: the people who follow me cannot endure to abandon their gods; but I shall go and speak to them according to your words.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Reims, the baptism at Christmas, three thousand behind him
stops.campa: The squares are shaded with tapestried canopies, the churches hung with white curtains; incense spreads, fragrant candles burn, and the baptistery fills with such perfume that the bystanders believe themselves amid the odors of paradise. The king asks to be baptized first: a new Constantine advances to the font to wash away the old leprosy. Remigius speaks the sentence over the bowed Sicambrian; Clovis, confessing God in Trinity, is anointed with chrism. More than three thousand of his army follow, and his sisters Albofled and Lantechild. In this same church the Maid will stand with her banner beside the Dauphin she crowns: his Reims faces Joan's.
stops.quote: Gently bend your neck, Sigamber; worship what you burned; burn what you worshipped.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Reims, Saint-Remi, the dove and the Holy Ampulla
stops.campa: The press of the crowd in the streets is so great that the clerk bearing the chrism cannot reach the font, and the holy oil is kept away. Remigius lifts his eyes, and a dove whiter than snow descends bearing in its beak a little vial of chrism sent from heaven; a fragrance beyond all incense fills the church, and with this oil the king is anointed. The vial is the Sainte Ampoule, kept at Saint-Remi: for thirteen hundred years it anoints the kings of France, down to the Dauphin whom Joan crowns in 1429 and the last king at Reims in 1825.

stops.name: Dijon, on the river Ouche, the brothers' battle
stops.campa: Godegisel, weary of his brother Gundobad's kingship, promises Clovis tribute in secret if he will help destroy him. Gundobad, ignorant of the treachery, calls his brother to his side against the Franks, and the three armies converge on the stronghold called Dijon. They fight on the Ouche; Godegisel goes over to Clovis in the midst of the battle, and together they crush Gundobad's people. Gundobad, seeing the treason of the brother he never suspected, turns and flees down the valley of the Rhône to shut himself in Avignon, while Godegisel enters Vienne in triumph as if the whole kingdom were already his.

stops.name: Avignon, the siege turned by the counsel of Aridius
stops.campa: Clovis sits with all his army around the walls, meaning to drag Gundobad out and slay him. But Gundobad's man Aridius, famed for energy and wisdom, feigns desertion and comes to the Frankish king, who keeps him close, for he is entertaining in storytelling, ready in counsel, just in judgment. Then, softly, Aridius talks the siege away: why hold an army against a strong place, ravaging fields you cannot eat? Clovis takes the advice, imposes a yearly tribute, and marches home. Gundobad pays, for a while, then besieges Godegisel in Vienne and kills him in an Arian church. Burgundy waits a generation for Clotilde's sons.
stops.quote: Send an embassy rather and impose tribute to be paid you every year, so that the country may be safe and you may rule forever over a tributary. And if he refuses, then do whatever pleases you.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.32 (trans. Brehaut), the counsel of Aridius

stops.name: The island of the Loire at Amboise, the two kings meet
stops.campa: Alaric, king of the Goths, watching Clovis conquer nations steadily, sends envoys asking for a meeting. Clovis does not spurn it. The two kings come to an island of the Loire near the village of Amboise in the territory of Tours, and there they talk and eat and drink together, plight friendship, and depart in peace. It is the peace of two swordsmen measuring the ground. Even at that time, Gregory writes, many in the Gauls desired greatly to have the Franks as masters: the Catholic south already leaning toward the baptized king across the river.
stops.quote: If my brother consents, it is the desire of my heart that with God's favor we have a meeting.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.35 (trans. Brehaut), Alaric's message

stops.name: Paris, the word against the Arians
stops.campa: Clovis speaks to his people the sentence that launches the conquest of Aquitaine: it grieves him that Arians hold a part of the Gauls. The words please them all. The army is set in motion toward Poitiers, where Alaric waits. In the register of the canon this is not politics but crusade before the word exists: the king baptized at Reims goes down against the heretic kingdom with the favor of God marching before him in signs: a psalm, a hind, a pillar of fire, each about to be given in its place.
stops.quote: I take it very hard that these Arians hold part of the Gauls. Let us go with God's help and conquer them and bring the land under our control.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: The border of Touraine, the edict of Saint Martin
stops.campa: As the host passes into Touraine, the king issues an edict out of respect for the blessed Martin: no one shall take anything from this country but grass for fodder and water. A soldier finds a poor man's hay and reasons like a lawyer: did not the king say grass? and is not hay grass? He takes it by force. Quicker than speech the man is slain by the sword, and the king speaks his fear over the body: the victory itself hangs on Martin's goodwill. It would be better, he says, for the army to take nothing at all from this country.
stops.quote: And where shall our hope of victory be if we offend the blessed Martin?
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Tours, basilica of Saint Martin, the omen of the psalm
stops.campa: The king sends envoys with gifts to the blessed church: go, he says, and perhaps you will receive some omen of victory from the holy temple, and he prays that if the Lord is his helper, He will consent to reveal it at the entrance. As the messengers step through the door of Saint Martin's, the first singer, without any pre-arrangement, lifts exactly this response into the air. They pay their vow to the blessed confessor and ride joyfully to the king: the omen is given, the unbelieving nation is surrendered into his hands.
stops.quote: Thou hast girded me, O Lord, with strength unto the battle; thou hast subdued under me those that rose up against me, and hast made mine enemies turn their backs unto me, and thou hast utterly destroyed them that hated me.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.37 (trans. Brehaut), the response sung at the door of Saint Martin's

stops.name: The ford of the Vienne, the hind shows the crossing (traditional site by Vieux-Poitiers)
stops.campa: The army comes to the river Vienne and cannot cross: the rains have swollen it and no man knows the ford. In the night the king prays to the Lord to show him a way over. In the morning, by God's will, a hind of wonderful size enters the river before the host, and where she passes the people see the shallow path and cross behind her, dry-shouldered, to the Poitiers bank. The God who parted a sea for Israel parts a river for the Franks with the body of a deer.

stops.name: Before Poitiers, the fire from Saint-Hilaire
stops.campa: Encamped within sight of Poitiers, the king in the night sees a ball of fire come out of the church of Saint Hilarius and pass, as it were, over him: the light of the blessed confessor, who in his lifetime fought the Arian heresy with the pen, now goes before the army that will fight it with iron. Clovis makes it known to the whole host that neither here nor on the road shall any man spoil or take another's property: the discipline of Touraine renewed on the eve of battle, so that no offense may dim the light that has chosen him.
